strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: defending LLM-based multi-agent systems without labeled malicious agents, which is a well-motivated relaxation of the supervised G-Safeguard paradigm and realistic for real-world deployments.

The proposed pipeline is clearly motivated via two identified gaps (multi-level context awareness; misaligned anomaly assumptions), and the design (hierarchical ego/neighbor/global aggregation, corruption-guided pseudo-anomalies with supervised contrastive training, similarity-based anomaly scoring, and edge-pruning remediation) is coherent and easy to follow.

Evaluation is broad: three attack types (prompt injection, tool attack, memory poisoning), four topologies (chain, tree, star, random), three LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-30B-A3B), multi-round ASR analysis (R1–R3), scalability to 20/50 agents, and an ablation of the hierarchical components, all following the established G-Safeguard setup.

The paper demonstrates a genuinely useful finding: a single unsupervised model trained only on normal interactions generalizes across attack types and even competes with a supervised upper bound in many settings (AUC > 80% in most cases), which supervised baselines cannot do without retraining per attack type.
Algorithm 1, optimizer details, and appendices provide enough implementation detail (hidden size, LR schedule, hardware) to support reproducibility, and the code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: The core assumption underlying the corruption-guided detector is under-validated: synthetic anomalies are generated by magnitude-scaled isotropic Gaussian noise in SentenceBERT embedding space (Eq. 5), which is a weak proxy for real semantic attacks (deceptive intent, misinformation, tool misuse). The paper criticizes prior GAD methods for misaligned anomaly assumptions (Gap 2), but never empirically analyzes why random embedding noise transfers to real malicious behaviors—e.g., no embedding-space analysis, sensitivity study over corruption intensity α, or comparison with text-level corruption alternatives.

Technical novelty is modest: the hierarchical encoder is a shallow one-layer aggregation (ego + neighbor mean + global mean fed to an MLP), inference-time scoring is simply negative average cosine similarity, and corruption-based contrastive training resembles standard feature-level noise augmentation. The contribution is largely a sensible re-combination of known components applied to MAS.

Missing baselines weaken the claims: there is no comparison with simple non-graph alternatives such as direct embedding-distance anomaly scoring on agent responses or LLM-as-judge detection, so the added value of the graph/hierarchical machinery relative to trivial approaches is not isolated (the ablation only removes NL/GL within the proposed model).

Statistical rigor is insufficient: no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported across the many repeated MAS rollouts (LLM outputs are stochastic), and it is unclear how many training/deployment MAS graphs are used or how many malicious agents are injected per graph.

Some empirical irregularities are not discussed: several unsupervised baselines report AUCs far below 50 (e.g., DOMINANT/TAM near 27–50), which suggests evaluation or feature-setup issues that deserve explanation; BlindGuard also underperforms PREM in some tool-attack settings (e.g., Random/TA AUC 79.56 vs 86.22) contrary to the general narrative.

The top-K anomaly budget (K=3) is somewhat arbitrary and its sensitivity is not analyzed; false-positive effects of pruning on benign MAS accuracy (clean performance without attacks) are not reported, which is important for a practical defense.

Presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is blank, 'PosionRAG'/'Leanrning' typos appear in figures/tables, and Figure 1/2 are dense; details on how tool and memory attacks are instantiated in the MAS simulator are deferred and thin.

Robustness against adaptive attacks (e.g., malicious agents that mimic normal response style to evade embedding-space detection) is not considered, which limits the strength of the 'unknown attacks' claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and timely problem: defending LLM-based multi-agent systems without requiring labeled malicious agents, which is a realistic limitation of prior supervised approaches (e.g., G-Safeguard).

The experimental scope is broad: three attack types (prompt injection, tool attack, memory poisoning), four communication topologies, multiple backbone LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3), and multi-round evaluation, following the established G-Safeguard evaluation protocol.

The proposed pipeline is simple and fully described (hierarchical feature concatenation, noise-based corruption, supervised contrastive loss, similarity-based anomaly scoring, edge pruning), making the approach easy to understand and implement in principle.

The ablation study (Figure 5) provides some evidence that neighborhood-level and global-level features contribute to detection performance, and the scalability experiment (Table 2) offers initial evidence at 20–50 agents.
The unsupervised paradigm claim is partially supported: BlindGuard consistently outperforms the three unsupervised GAD baselines (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM) on most settings.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The 'hierarchical agent encoder' reduces to concatenating ego features, a one-hop neighborhood mean, and a global mean (Eq. 3–4) with no learned aggregation; the corruption strategy is isotropic Gaussian noise scaled by feature magnitude; the anomaly score is negative average cosine similarity. Each component is a straightforward instantiation of existing techniques, and the paper does not articulate why this particular design is well-suited to semantic adversarial behavior beyond intuition.

A critical missing baseline: the paper never compares against simply applying the contextual similarity anomaly score (Eq. 7) directly on frozen SentenceBERT embeddings without any contrastive training. Without this ablation, the central claim that corruption-guided contrastive learning is essential is unsupported—it is unclear how much of the performance comes from the learned detector versus the off-the-shelf encoder plus similarity scoring.

Unvalidated core assumption. The method assumes real malicious agent behavior manifests as embedding-space deviation comparable to random noise corruption (Eq. 5). No qualitative or quantitative analysis (e.g., t-SNE visualization of real attacked vs. normal agents, sensitivity of results to α) substantiates that synthetic noise corruption is a faithful proxy for prompt injection, memory poisoning, or tool exploitation, which may not produce detectable text-level deviations at all.

The gap to the supervised upper bound is large (G-Safeguard AUC ≈ 98–100 vs. BlindGuard ≈ 60–85), and the paper's claim of 'comparable effectiveness' is overstated. On several settings (e.g., PI-GSM8k, TA-InjecAgent on Random, PI-CSQA on Chain), BlindGuard's ASR@3 is actually worse than individual unsupervised baselines, which conflicts with the 'significantly outperforms' framing.

Reproducibility concerns: the code URL in the abstract is empty. Key hyperparameters are not reported in the main text or appendix (corruption intensity α, corruption ratio, contrastive temperature τ, number of training graphs, number of random seeds), and no variance or statistical significance is reported across repeated runs despite ASR differences between methods often being within a few percentage points.

Insufficient methodological details on the training data: how much 'normal MAS interaction data' is needed, how it is collected, and how sensitive performance is to this distribution shift relative to the deployment MAS are not analyzed—yet this is central to the claimed practical advantage.

Detection is based solely on agent response text (SentenceBERT of R_i). The connection between attack type and detectable signal is not analyzed; for tool exploitation and memory poisoning, malicious behavior may not surface in inter-agent messages, and the paper provides no error analysis or failure cases.

Scalability claims are weak: 'scaling to larger MAS' involves only 20 vs. 50 agents, which is far from realistic large-scale deployments, and the explanation ('topology-agnostic design') is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Presentation issues undermine clarity: the direct URL is missing, 'PosionRAG' is misspelled throughout, Figure 2 contains typos ('Leanrning'), Table 1 includes a tool-attack result where BlindGuard is not the best unsupervised method but the text claims uniform superiority, and Figure 1's motivation (supervised model trained on PI failing on MA) is not directly supported by an experiment isolating cross-attack-type transfer of G-Safeguard.
No comparison with LLM-based or prompt-based detection approaches (e.g., asking the LLM to judge suspicious messages), which are natural and practical alternatives in this setting.

strengths: Well-motivated and practical problem setting: removing the reliance on labeled malicious agents for MAS defense is a genuine and important gap relative to supervised approaches like G-Safeguard, and the unsupervised paradigm is clearly formulated.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper tests across 3 attack types (prompt injection, tool attack, memory poisoning), 4 communication topologies (chain, tree, star, random), multiple datasets (CSQA, MMLU, GSM8K, InjecAgent, PoisonRAG), and 3 LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-30B-A3B), which is a strong breadth of evidence for a security paper.

The corruption-guided detector trained with supervised contrastive learning on only normal data is a sensible, lightweight strategy, and the universal-model experiments (one model defending against both PI and MA on the same dataset) directly support the generalization claim.
Ablation study (RQ4) and scalability experiments (20 vs. 50 agents, multi-round R1–R3 results in the appendix) provide supporting evidence for the design choices and practical deployment claims.
The paper is generally well written, clearly structured around research questions, with sufficient algorithmic detail (Algorithm 1) and appendices covering related work, setup, and extended results.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the hierarchical encoder reduces to concatenating ego features, a 1-hop normalized mean, and a global mean followed by an MLP (essentially an SGC-style summarization), and the training objective is a standard supervised contrastive loss. The conceptual contribution is the reframing (corruption-as-pseudo-anomalies), not a deep methodological advance.

An internal tension in the threat-model assumptions: the Preliminary states that attacked agents 'maintain superficial operational normality', yet the corruption-based simulation assumes malicious agents produce semantically deviated responses detectable as embedding-space outliers. Camouflaged or subtle attacks (e.g., memory poisoning with plausible content) may not exhibit the random-noise-like deviation that Gaussian corruption in SentenceBERT space simulates. No analysis of this assumption's validity is provided.

The anomaly score (negative average similarity to all agents) risks conflating benign but atypical agents (unusual roles, verbose styles, out-of-domain questions) with attackers. There is no false-positive analysis or evaluation on clean, non-attacked MAS, which is critical for a defense method.

Some results weaken the headline claims: BlindGuard is often 15–25 AUC points below the supervised G-Safeguard (e.g., 79.11 vs. 100 on Chain PI-CSQA), loses in AUC to DOMINANT on TA-InjecAgent (Chain), and in several ASR cells trails individual baselines. Phrases like 'significantly outperforms other unsupervised methods' and 'comparable effectiveness in most cases' are somewhat stronger than the tables fully support, and no statistical significance or variance across runs is reported.

Evaluation protocol details are under-specified: the top-3 budget assumes a fixed number of malicious agents per MAS, but the actual number and ratio of malicious agents per system, and the effect of the budget on precision/recall, are not clarified. Sensitivity to the corruption intensity hyperparameter α is also not analyzed.

The practical assumption of access to 'normal MAS interaction data' for training deserves more discussion: how much data is needed, how it is collected, and whether domain shift between training and deployment scenarios (different tasks, agent roles, prompts) hurts detection are not examined.

Reproducibility is undermined by an incomplete code link (the URL in the abstract is blank), and key training-data statistics (number of normal graphs, dataset sizes for training) are missing from the main text.

The discussion of closely related concurrent defenses (e.g., A-Trust) is relegated entirely to the appendix, and there is no comparison against generation/judge-based defenses (e.g., LLM-as-judge filtering), which would clarify the value of the graph-based approach.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: unsupervised (label-free) defense of LLM-based multi-agent systems against unknown attacks, clearly positioning itself against the supervised G-Safeguard paradigm and articulating two concrete gaps (multi-level contextual awareness; misaligned anomaly assumptions) in existing GAD methods.

The methodology is well-motivated and clearly described: a hierarchical agent encoder (ego / neighborhood / global views over SentenceBERT features), a corruption-based attack simulation in embedding space, supervised contrastive training, and similarity-based anomaly scoring with edge-pruning remediation. Algorithm 1, complexity analysis, and hyperparameter details support reproducibility.

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive: 4 topologies, 3 attack types across 5 datasets, 3 LLM backbones (including weaker Qwen3-8B), 20/50-agent scaling, ablations of encoder components and the raw-SBERT baseline, corruption-intensity sensitivity, threshold-based (unknown-K) remediation, attack-free utility checks, plus dedicated collusion and adaptive-attack experiments — an honest robustness effort beyond the standard setup.

The supervised baseline is treated fairly as an upper bound, and the claim that unsupervised training generalizes better to unseen attack types (Table 2) is a genuinely interesting and well-supported empirical finding.

The appendix includes a candid failure-case analysis (false positives from benign style heterogeneity, false negatives from on-topic manifold-preserving mimicry) and a limitations section, which increases credibility.
Writing and figures are generally clear; the code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: The unsupervised setting still assumes access to a clean set of benign MAS interaction graphs for training. The paper does not discuss how realistic this assumption is in deployment (contaminated training data, distribution shift between training and deployed systems), which weakens the central practicality claim relative to G-Safeguard.

There is an internal inconsistency in the core corruption mechanism: Eq. 5 injects isotropic Gaussian noise with random direction (epsilon ~ N(0, I)), yet the framing and Appendix H describe 'semantics-aware directional negatives.' The claimed angular-margin argument about attacks deviating in specific directions is not clearly instantiated by the actual training corruption, so the mechanism's alignment with real semantic attacks remains asserted rather than demonstrated.

The method itself is a fairly straightforward combination of known components (frozen SentenceBERT features, neighborhood/global mean pooling, supervised contrastive loss with synthetic corruptions, mean-cosine anomaly scoring). While effective, the technical novelty is moderate and the ablation showing raw SBERT + Eq. 7 already reaches AUC ~67-77 suggests a large share of performance comes from embeddings rather than the learned encoder.

Evaluation leaks knowledge of the attack structure: exactly 3 agents are compromised in all test scenarios and the detection budget K=3 matches this. The threshold variant in E.3 partially mitigates this, but AUC computation and ASR comparisons under the matched budget favor all top-K detectors; more diverse attacker counts would strengthen the claims.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance across seeds is reported anywhere, despite LLM-based MAS experiments being inherently noisy; it is unclear how many seeds were run and whether gaps between BlindGuard and baselines (which are sometimes small) are reliable.

ASR reductions over the strongest unsupervised baselines are modest in several settings (e.g., PI tasks in random topology), and AUC remains far below the supervised upper bound on some attack types; the paper could more precisely characterize when the unsupervised approach is and is not adequate.

Minor presentation issues: typos (e.g., 'Denfesnse' in Figure 2, 'Such the single-purpose design'), several suspicious 2026-dated citations, and occasional overclaiming in prose (e.g., 'extensively evaluate under rigorous real-world conditions' while the evaluation is entirely simulated).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem: defending LLM-based multi-agent systems without requiring labeled malicious agents, which meaningfully relaxes the assumptions of the closest prior work (G-Safeguard).

The evaluation is unusually broad for this line of work: four topologies, three attack families across five datasets, three LLM backbones, scalability to 20/50 agents, ablations, threshold-based and fixed-budget variants, collusion and adaptive attacks, attack-free utility checks, and an honest failure case analysis.
The method is fully specified (Eq. 2-9, Algorithm 1), with complexity analysis and hyperparameter sensitivity reported, supporting reproducibility in principle; code availability is promised.

The unsupervised paradigm is shown to generalize better than the supervised upper bound to unseen attack types (Table 2), which substantiates the central motivation rather than merely the accuracy claim.
The limitation and failure analysis (Appendix I) is candid and technically informative, distinguishing stealthy on-topic attacks from false positives caused by benign reasoning-style heterogeneity.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is thin relative to the framing. The 'hierarchical agent encoder' reduces to concatenating the ego embedding, a 1-hop mean, and a global mean through an MLP (Eq. 3-4), and inference (Eq. 7) is simply negative average cosine similarity to all other agents. This is close to vanilla embedding-space OOD detection plus edge pruning, and the paper overstates its novelty.

There is a substantive inconsistency between claims and the actual mechanism: the method and Appendix H repeatedly describe 'semantics-aware directional negatives' and an angular margin aligned with how attacks deviate, but Eq. 5 injects isotropic Gaussian noise (direction drawn uniformly at random), which is not attack-direction-aware. Appendix H even acknowledges isotropic noise 'does not provide such targeted boundary refinement.' This undermines a core claimed design rationale and Gap-2 argument.

The evaluation protocol has soundness concerns: exactly 3 agents are compromised and the detection budget is K=3, so ASR is nearly a deterministic function of top-3 detection; AUC over graphs with tens of nodes is a high-variance estimate. No seeds, variance, or significance testing are reported, so several margins over baselines (and over G-Safeguard in Table 2) may not be reliable.

Simulated environments only, with fixed 3-of-N compromise scenarios and template-based attacks; 'rigorous real-world conditions' (Section 2 contributions) is an overclaim, and adaptive-attack coverage is limited to a single hand-designed PI variant.

Presentation quality is below par: typos (e.g., 'Denfesnse' in Figure 2, grammatical slips in Section 3.4 and RQ4), and the reference list contains numerous implausibly future-dated entries (e.g., arXiv:2602.18793, arXiv:2604.06834, AAAI volume 40 in 2026), which raises concerns about reference hygiene that should be corrected.

The framing relies on a strawman to some degree: supervised G-Safeguard is used as an 'upper bound' while its generalization failure is emphasized, but no supervised multi-attack training baseline (trained on mixed attack types) is included, which is the fairer comparator for the generalizability claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem: defending LLM-based multi-agent systems without labeled malicious agents, which meaningfully extends the G-Safeguard supervised paradigm to a more realistic unsupervised setting.

The proposed method is clearly motivated by two well-articulated gaps (multi-level contextual awareness; misaligned anomaly assumptions), and the hierarchical encoder (ego/neighbor/global) plus corruption-guided contrastive detector directly target them.

The experimental campaign is unusually comprehensive: 4 topologies, 3 attack modalities across 5 datasets, 3 LLM backbones, scalability to 20/50 agents, ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, attack-free utility checks, threshold vs. top-K variants, collusion and adaptive attacks, and an honest failure-case analysis.

The unsupervised method approaches the supervised upper bound (G-Safeguard) in most settings and clearly beats adapted GAD baselines (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM), supporting the central claim that label-free MAS defense is feasible.
The paper is generally well organized, includes complexity analysis, algorithmic pseudocode, and claims code release, supporting reproducibility at a reasonable level.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the encoder is essentially concatenation of ego features, 1-hop mean, and global mean fed to an MLP, and the detector is Gaussian noise injection into SentenceBERT embeddings trained with standard supervised contrastive loss (Khosla et al., 2020). Each component is well-executed but largely a recombination of existing techniques.

There is an internal inconsistency in the corruption mechanism: Eq. (5) injects directionally uniform (isotropic-direction) noise, yet Appendix G/H describe 'semantics-aware directional negatives.' The methodology section and the justification appendix do not fully align, which weakens the theoretical story.

The core assumption—that malicious agents produce semantically deviated responses detectable via embedding shift—is strong and the paper itself shows (Appendix H, I) that manifold-preserving, on-topic attacks evade detection; the adaptive-attack test (Table 8) uses only one fairly simple strategy, so robustness claims against 'unknown attacks' are only partially substantiated.

Residual attack success rates remain substantial (e.g., ASR@3 of ~20-30% for PI on several topologies), and the claim of 'AUC>80% in most cases' does not hold uniformly (e.g., PI GSM8k AUC drops to ~59-75), so the headline results should be stated more carefully.

Evaluation assumes oracle knowledge of the number of compromised agents (K=3) in the main results; although K=2 and threshold variants are relegated to the appendix, this setting weakens the realism claim for the primary tables.

No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported for any experiment, despite LLM-based simulations being noisy; it is unclear whether several small AUC/ASR differences are meaningful.

Reproducibility gaps: the code link is a placeholder ('Code'), the amount and construction of normal training MAS data is under-specified, and there are editorial quality issues (typos such as 'BlinGuard', 'Denfesnse'; several citations with implausible/future arXiv identifiers) that suggest the manuscript needs another careful pass.

The comparison set for unsupervised baselines is narrow (three generic GAD methods); there is no comparison to simpler unsupervised alternatives such as LLM-judge or self-consistency-based detection, making it hard to judge whether the full pipeline is necessary versus the learned encoder alone (though Table 9 partially addresses this).
